clinicalPearls: A true osteonecrosis of the capitellum affecting its developing ossification centre, not a traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the capitellum of the distal humerus at the lateral elbow
Typically affects young children, roughly five to ten years of age, often in the dominant throwing arm
Presents with dull lateral elbow pain, stiffness and a mild flexion contracture, worse with throwing or weight-bearing on the arm
The radiographic hallmark is irregularity, fragmentation and sclerosis of the capitellar ossification centre, sometimes with later reossification
It should be distinguished from osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, which occurs in older adolescents and can produce loose bodies
Unlike osteochondritis dissecans, Panner disease usually involves the whole ossific nucleus and tends to reconstitute with growth
Management is conservative with rest, activity modification and avoidance of throwing, with physiotherapy to restore motion as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Panner disease is an osteochondrosis of the capitellum in which the ossification centre of the lateral distal humerus undergoes ischaemic change during childhood. Repetitive valgus and compressive loading of the immature elbow, particularly from throwing or upper limb weight-bearing, is thought to disturb the blood supply to the developing capitellum. This produces necrosis, fragmentation and sclerosis of the ossific nucleus, followed by revascularisation and reossification as growth continues. Because the process typically affects the entire ossification centre in a skeletally immature child and remodels with growth, it is generally self-limiting, in contrast to capitellar osteochondritis dissecans in older adolescents, which involves a focal osteochondral fragment and carries a higher risk of loose bodies and residual joint incongruity.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the elbow
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the elbow
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and lateral elbow radiographs showing capitellar fragmentation and sclerosis
Comparison views of the contralateral elbow to gauge normal ossification
Magnetic resonance imaging to assess the articular cartilage and distinguish from osteochondritis dissecans
Assessment of elbow range of motion and any fixed flexion contracture
Inflammatory markers if infection or inflammatory arthritis is suspected
Follow-up imaging to confirm reossification of the capitellum
redFlags: Mechanical locking or catching suggesting a loose body and osteochondritis dissecans rather than Panner disease
Progressive fixed flexion contracture or loss of motion
Systemic features or joint effusion raising concern for infection or inflammatory arthritis
Persistent symptoms in an older adolescent, which favour osteochondritis dissecans with poorer prognosis
reference.prognosis: Panner disease generally carries a favourable prognosis; the capitellum usually reossifies and remodels with growth once the elbow is rested, and most children recover full or near-full function without long-term joint damage.
pitfalls: Confusing Panner disease with capitellar osteochondritis dissecans, which has a different age group and worse outlook
Allowing continued throwing, which perpetuates loading of the healing capitellum
Missing an alternative diagnosis such as infection when an effusion or systemic features are present
Failing to arrange follow-up imaging to confirm reossification
management: Rest and activity modification, stopping throwing and upper-limb weight-bearing until symptoms settle, the mainstay of treatment
Simple analgesia or NSAIDs and ice for pain during the symptomatic phase
Short-term immobilisation or splinting of the elbow if pain is marked
Gentle range-of-motion exercises and physiotherapy to address stiffness and any flexion contracture
Serial radiographs to confirm reossification and remodelling of the capitellum
Distinguish from and monitor for osteochondritis dissecans with loose bodies in the older child, referring to orthopaedics if atypical or non-resolving
Graded return to sport once pain-free with restored range of motion

Red flag (locking, progressive contracture, effusion or systemic features)?
Escalate: orthopaedic review for loose body or infection
AP and lateral elbow radiographs, contralateral comparison, MRI if uncertain
Do radiographs show capitellar fragmentation in a young child without locking?
Consider capitellar OCD, medial apophysitis, radial head fracture or septic arthritis
Rest from throwing and upper-limb weight-bearing until symptoms settle
